mainTopic: Forgiving a זקן ממרא, the ladder of courts, when a זקן ממרא becomes liable, and why only תפילין fits his liability
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא: parents may forgive a בן סורר ומורה, but the חכמים of the South refused to let a court forgive a זקן ממרא, so that disputes would not spread in ישראל. The גמרא calls this a תיובתא. רבי יוסי then describes how courts once kept the law united. A question climbed from the local court, to the courts at the הר הבית and the עזרה, and up to the great court in the לשכת הגזית, which answered from tradition or by majority vote. Disputes multiplied only when students of שמאי and הלל did not serve their teachers enough. The ברייתא also explains how wise, humble judges were promoted up the same ladder, and a message from ארץ ישראל describes who is fit for עולם הבא. The גמרא then asks what is new about a זקן ממרא who acts on his own ruling. It answers that he no longer needs a warning, and for a מסית, his excuse is no longer accepted. A new משנה teaches that he is liable only for adding to rulings of the Sages, like a fifth box in תפילין. רבי אושעיא says only תפילין fits this rule, and the גמרא shows why לולב does not fit. Its answer about ציצית continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Parents may forgive a rebellious son
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא being quoted continues its list: if the parents of a בן סורר ומורה want to forgive him, they may.
steps.simpleTranslation: A stubborn and rebellious son whose father and mother wanted to forgive him: they may forgive him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing a ברייתא it began quoting earlier. This line gives the second case on the list: parents can forgive a בן סורר ומורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בן סורר ומורה is only judged if his parents bring him to court. So if they choose to forgive him, the case simply stops. This case is a lead-in to the case the גמרא really cares about, the זקן ממרא.

keyTerms.meaning: The stubborn and rebellious son described in the תורה
To forgive or pardon
They may forgive him

phrases.english: A stubborn and rebellious son,
whose father and mother wanted to forgive him –
they may forgive him.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּן סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה, שֶׁרָצוּ אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ לִמְחוֹל לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא whose first case was quoted before this section begins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Parents may forgive a בן סורר ומורה.

steps.title: The speaker says a court may forgive a rebellious elder
steps.stepSummary: The third case: the speaker of the ברייתא holds that a זקן ממרא's own court may forgive him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A rebellious elder whose court wanted to forgive him: they may forgive him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its third case: the speaker's own opinion that a court may forgive a זקן ממרא. This sets up the twist that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A זקן ממרא is a sage who rules against the great court in practice. The speaker thinks the court that was defied may let it go, just like parents with a son. But the next line will show that the other חכמים did not accept this.

keyTerms.meaning: A rebellious elder who rules in practice against the great בית דין
His court, the court whose ruling he defied

phrases.aramaic: זָקֵן מַמְרֵא שֶׁרָצוּ בֵּית דִּינוֹ לִמְחוֹל לוֹ –
phrases.english: A rebellious elder whose court wanted to forgive him –
they may forgive him.

steps.triggerLanguage: זָקֵן מַמְרֵא שֶׁרָצוּ בֵּית דִּינוֹ לִמְחוֹל לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the third case to the same list, using the same pattern.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the speaker's own view, a court may forgive a זקן ממרא.

steps.title: The southern sages refused forgiveness for a rebellious elder
steps.stepSummary: The speaker reports that his colleagues in the South accepted two of his cases but rejected forgiveness for a זקן ממרא, so that מחלוקות would not multiply.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I came to my colleagues in the South, they agreed with me about two cases, but they did not agree with me about the rebellious elder, so that disputes should not multiply in Israel.
steps.whatsHappening: The speaker admits that the other חכמים rejected his view on the זקן ממרא. They held that his court may not forgive him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The colleagues explain why: if a court could excuse a sage who defies it, disputes would spread through ישראל. So the accepted position in the ברייתא is that a זקן ממרא is not forgiven. This is what the גמרא uses as proof in the next line.

keyTerms.meaning: My colleagues in the South
They agreed with me
Disputes, disagreements

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives the reason behind the strict rule: the authority of the great court protects ישראל from splitting into many conflicting practices.

phrases.english: And when I came to my colleagues in the South,
about two they agreed with me,
phrases.notes: The two are the other cases on the list, including the בן סורר ומורה.

phrases.aramaic: עַל זָקֵן מַמְרֵא לֹא הוֹדוּ לִי,
phrases.english: about the rebellious elder they did not agree with me,
so that disputes should not multiply in Israel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reverses the speaker's view from step 2 by reporting that his colleagues rejected it.
steps.raayaObject: The view that a זקן ממרא may not be forgiven by his court.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The southern sages in the ברייתא rejected forgiveness for a זקן ממרא so that מחלוקות would not multiply.

steps.title: A conclusive refutation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares a תיובתא: the view that a זקן ממרא can be forgiven is refuted.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a conclusive refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the discussion with one word: the opinion that a court may forgive a זקן ממרא has been refuted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the סוגיא there was a dispute about whether a court can forgive a זקן ממרא. Since the ברייתא shows the חכמים refused, the view that allowed forgiveness cannot stand. The view of רבי אלעזר, that he is not forgiven, holds.

keyTerms.meaning: A conclusive refutation; the opposing view is knocked down

steps.whatToRemember: A זקן ממרא is not forgiven, even if his own court wants to forgive him, so that disputes do not spread in ישראל.
steps.confusionAlert: The speaker of the ברייתא did allow forgiveness, but the refutation comes from the colleagues who rejected him. Their view is the one that decides the question.

phrases.english: A conclusive refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the final result from the colleagues' rejection in step 3.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The opinion that a court may forgive a זקן ממרא is refuted; he is not forgiven.

steps.title: רבי יוסי describes the original court system
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי teaches that originally there were few disputes, because of an organized system: the great court of seventy-one, two courts of twenty-three at the הר הבית and the עזרה, and courts in every city.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught: רבי יוסי said: At first, disputes did not multiply in Israel. Rather, the court of seventy-one sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, two courts of twenty-three sat at the entrances of the Temple Mount and the Temple courtyard, and the other courts of twenty-three sat in all the cities of Israel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא from רבי יוסי. It sets up a picture of how the courts were arranged, to prepare for explaining how questions were settled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to the theme just mentioned, keeping מחלוקות from spreading. רבי יוסי explains that the courts were arranged in levels. The next step will show how a question moved up through these levels.

keyTerms.meaning: It is taught in a ברייתא
The Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the great סנהדרין sat
The Temple Mount
The Temple courtyard
Twenty-three, the size of a smaller סנהדרין

phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Yosei said:
At first, disputes did not multiply in Israel,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the meaning stays the same.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל שִׁבְעִים וְאֶחָד
phrases.english: rather, the court of seventy-one
would sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone,

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁנֵי בָּתֵּי דִינִין שֶׁל עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה,
phrases.english: and two courts of twenty-three,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד יוֹשֵׁב עַל פֶּתַח הַר הַבַּיִת
phrases.english: one sat at the entrance of the Temple Mount
and one sat at the entrance of the Temple courtyard,

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁאָר בָּתֵּי דִינִין שֶׁל עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה
phrases.english: and the other courts of twenty-three
would sit in all the cities of Israel.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: מִתְּחִילָּה לֹא הָיוּ מַחְלוֹקוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the theme of preventing מחלוקות and describes the court system that kept them from spreading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Originally the courts were arranged in levels, from local courts up to the great court of seventy-one in the לשכת הגזית.

steps.title: How a question climbed from court to court
steps.stepSummary: A question went first to the local court, then a nearby court, then the court at the הר הבית, then the court at the עזרה, until someone had a clear tradition.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a matter needed to be asked, they asked the court in their city. If they had heard a ruling, they told them. If not, they came to the court near their city. If they had heard, they told them. If not, they came to the court at the entrance of the Temple Mount. If they had heard, they told them. If not, they came to the court at the entrance of the Temple courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי continues and explains the step-by-step path a question took. At each level, if the court had a clear tradition, it answered; if not, the question moved one level higher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key word is 'heard': a court answered only if it had a received tradition, not a guess. Because unclear questions moved up instead of each court deciding on its own, disputes did not spread. The ladder continues past the עזרה in the next part of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter needed to be asked
If they had heard (a clear tradition)
And if not
Near their city

phrases.english: If the matter needed to be asked,
they would ask the court in their city.
If they had heard, they told them.
phrases.notes: 'Heard' means they had a clear tradition from their teachers about this question.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו, בָּאִין לָזֶה שֶׁסָּמוּךְ לְעִירָן.
phrases.english: And if not, they would come to the court near their city.
If they had heard, they told them.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו, בָּאִין לָזֶה שֶׁעַל פֶּתַח הַר הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: And if not, they would come to the one at the entrance of the Temple Mount.
If they had heard, they told them.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו, בָּאִין לָזֶה שֶׁעַל פֶּתַח הָעֲזָרָה.
phrases.english: And if not, they would come to the one at the entrance of the Temple courtyard.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּצְרַךְ הַדָּבָר לִשְׁאוֹל, שׁוֹאֲלִין מִבֵּית דִּין שֶׁבְּעִירָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the court structure from step 5 to describe the order in which questions were brought.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unclear question moved up the court ladder level by level until a court with a clear tradition answered it.

steps.title: The disagreeing elder lays out both views, and the question goes up to the great court
steps.stepSummary: At the court at the entrance of the עזרה, the elder who disagrees presents his reasoning next to his colleagues' reasoning. If that court has a tradition, it answers. If not, both sides go up to the לשכת הגזית, where the great court sits all day.
steps.simpleTranslation: The elder says: 'This is how I explained it, and this is how my colleagues explained it. This is what I taught, and this is what my colleagues taught.' If the court had heard a clear answer, they told them. If not, both groups came to the לשכת הגזית, where the court sat from the morning תמיד until the afternoon תמיד.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא describes what happens at the court at the entrance of the עזרה, where the elder sets out both views. If that court has no clear tradition, the question goes to the very top court, the לשכת הגזית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The elder does not simply announce that he is right. He sets out both explanations side by side so the court can judge. The final stop is the great court of seventy-one, which sits throughout the hours of the daily offerings.

keyTerms.meaning: I explained it (by interpreting the text)
I taught (what I received or decided)
The Chamber of Hewn Stone, seat of the great סנהדרין
The daily morning offering

phrases.english: And he says: This is how I expounded
phrases.notes: 'He' is the elder whose view differs from his colleagues'. The ברייתא hasn't named him yet.

phrases.english: and this is how my colleagues expounded;
this is what I taught
and this is what my colleagues taught.
If they had heard, they told them.
phrases.notes: The judges of the court being asked had heard a clear tradition, so they simply give the answer.

phrases.english: And if not, these and those come
to the Chamber of Hewn Stone,
where they sit from the daily morning offering
until the daily afternoon offering.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאוֹמֵר: כָּךְ דָּרַשְׁתִּי וְכָךְ דָּרְשׁוּ חֲבֵירַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues step 6's ladder of courts and describes the final stop, the לשכת הגזית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A question no lower court can answer from tradition goes up to the great court in the לשכת הגזית, which sits from the morning תמיד to the afternoon תמיד.

steps.title: How the great court decides: tradition first, then a majority vote
steps.stepSummary: On שבת and יום טוב the court sits at the חיל. When a question comes, they answer from tradition if they have one. Otherwise they vote, and the majority decides.
steps.simpleTranslation: On שבת and יום טוב they sat at the חיל. When a question was asked before them, they answered if they had heard a tradition. If not, they stood for a vote. If more judges said impure, they ruled it impure. If more said pure, they ruled it pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains where the great court sits on holy days and how it settles a question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to decide: a received tradition, or a vote. Because the great court always reaches a final majority ruling, the question ends there and no lasting dispute remains.

keyTerms.meaning: The rampart, an area on the הר הבית just outside the wall of the עזרה
They stand for a count, meaning they vote
Those who rule something impure
Those who rule something pure

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why there used to be few disputes. The top court always gave a final answer, by tradition or by majority.

phrases.english: And on Shabbatot and Festivals,
they sit at the rampart.
When a question was asked before them,
if they had heard, they told them;
and if not, they stand for a count.
If those declaring it impure were the majority, they declared it impure;
if those declaring it pure were the majority, they declared it pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds where the great court sits on holy days and how it reaches a final decision.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the great court has no tradition, it votes, and the majority's ruling becomes the law.

steps.title: Why disputes multiplied: students who did not serve their teachers enough
steps.stepSummary: Once the students of שמאי and הלל who had not served their teachers enough grew in number, disputes multiplied, and the תורה became like two תורות.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the students of שמאי and הלל who had not served their teachers as much as they needed became many, disputes multiplied in Israel, and the תורה became like two תורות.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא returns to the point רבי יוסי began with. Disputes used to be few, so it now explains how they grew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The system of courts kept the law unified. Once many students had not learned closely enough from their teachers, they lacked clear traditions, so disagreements spread. The result was two separate bodies of practice.

keyTerms.meaning: The students of שמאי and הלל
Served their teachers, learning closely from them
Like two separate תורות

steps.whatToRemember: Earlier there were few disputes because of the courts' system. Disputes multiplied when students did not learn closely enough from their teachers.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not blaming שמאי and הלל themselves. It is talking about students who did not serve them enough.

phrases.english: Once the students of Shammai and Hillel increased
who did not serve as much as they needed,
phrases.notes: 'Serve' means attending their teachers, which is how a student picks up the teacher's traditions.

phrases.english: disputes increased in Israel
and the Torah became like two Torahs.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשֶּׁרַבּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי שַׁמַּאי וְהִלֵּל שֶׁלֹּא שִׁמְּשׁוּ כׇּל צָרְכָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5's opening point by explaining how the early state of few disputes ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Disputes multiplied because students of שמאי and הלל did not serve their teachers sufficiently.

steps.title: How judges were chosen and promoted up the court ladder
steps.stepSummary: The great court sends word everywhere: a person who is wise, humble and liked by people should be a judge in his city. From there he is promoted to the court at the הר הבית, then the עזרה, then the לשכת הגזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: From there they write and send to every place: anyone who is wise, humble, and whom people are comfortable with should be a judge in his city. From there they promote him to the הר הבית, from there to the עזרה, and from there to the לשכת הגזית.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא goes back to describing the great court and explains how judges were appointed and moved up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judges move up the same ladder that questions travel in step 6: city, הר הבית, עזרה, לשכת הגזית. A judge needs good character and people's trust, not only wisdom.

keyTerms.meaning: Humble (literally, low of knee)
People are comfortable with him
A judge
They promote, raising him to a higher court

steps.whatToRemember: Judges climbed the same four-level ladder as questions: city court, הר הבית, עזרה, לשכת הגזית. They had to be wise, humble and trusted.

phrases.english: From there they write and send to all places:
phrases.notes: 'From there' means from the great court in the לשכת הגזית, not from the line about disputes just before.

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מִי שֶׁהוּא חָכָם, וּשְׁפַל בֶּרֶךְ,
phrases.english: Anyone who is wise and humble,
and people's minds are at ease with him,
shall be a judge in his city.
From there they promote him to the Temple Mount,
phrases.notes: He is promoted to the court of twenty-three at the הר הבית from step 5.

phrases.english: from there to the Temple courtyard,
from there to the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to describing the great court's workings, now about appointing and promoting judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wise, humble person whom people trust is appointed judge in his city and promoted step by step up to the לשכת הגזית.

steps.title: Who is fit for עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: A message from ארץ ישראל lists the traits of a person fit for עולם הבא. The Sages saw these traits in רב עולא בר אבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent from ארץ ישראל: Who is fit for עולם הבא? A person who is modest and humble, who bows as he comes in and bows as he goes out, who learns תורה all the time, and who does not take credit for himself. The Sages saw this in רב עולא בר אבא.
steps.whatsHappening: Right after describing the kind of person who should be a judge, the גמרא brings a related message from ארץ ישראל. It describes the kind of person who is fit for עולם הבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said a judge must be wise, humble and liked by people. This message adds a picture of true humility: bowing when coming and going, learning all the time, and never taking credit. The Sages point to a real person, רב עולא בר אבא, as the example.

keyTerms.meaning: A person fit for the World to Come
A modest, humble person
Humble (literally, 'low of knee')
Learns תורה
Takes credit for himself

phrases.english: They sent from there:
phrases.notes: 'There' means ארץ ישראל. The Sages there sent this message to בבל.

phrases.english: Who is one fit for the World to Come?
One who is modest and humble,
who bows as he enters and bows as he leaves,
and learns Torah all the time,
and does not take credit for himself.
The Sages set their eyes on him,
on Rav Ulla bar Abba.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds to the description of the humble, worthy judge in Step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person fit for עולם הבא is humble, bows when coming and going, learns תורה all the time, and does not take credit. The Sages saw this in רב עולא בר אבא.

steps.title: When the rebellious elder becomes liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה line 'he returned to his city and taught,' then brings a ברייתא. The זקן ממרא is liable only if he acts on his ruling, or if others act on his ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: he went back to his city and taught. A ברייתא teaches: he is not liable until he acts on his ruling himself, or until he rules for others and they act on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about the זקן ממרא who goes home and keeps teaching his view. It brings a ברייתא that spells out exactly when he becomes liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just teaching his view is not enough to make him liable. There must be action: either he does it himself, or others do it because of his ruling. The ברייתא names two ways he can become liable, and this sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: He returned to his city and taught (a line from the משנה)
The Rabbis taught (opens a ברייתא)
A halachic ruling
The rebellious elder who rules against the great court

steps.confusionAlert: Teaching his view alone does not make him liable. He becomes liable only when someone acts on his ruling, either he himself or others.

phrases.english: He returned to his city and taught.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה about the זקן ממרא who goes home and keeps teaching his own view.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
He is not liable until he acts on his ruling,
or until he rules for others
and they act on his ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה כְּהוֹרָאָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and goes back to the laws of the זקן ממרא in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The זקן ממרא is liable only if he acts on his ruling, or if he rules for others and they act on it.

steps.title: Why is acting on his own ruling anything new
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees that liability for others acting on his ruling is new. But if he does the sin himself, he was already liable to death before he became a זקן ממרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense when he rules for others and they act on it. Before, he could not be killed for that, and now he can. But when he acts on his ruling himself, he could already be killed for it before!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first part of the ברייתא. Why does it need to say he is liable when he acts on his own ruling?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Telling others to sin normally does not carry the death penalty, so making him liable for that is a real new rule. But a person who does a sin that carries death is already liable for doing it. So what does his status as a זקן ממרא add?

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it makes sense (opens a challenge)
At first, before
Liable to be put to death
Now

phrases.english: Granted, when he rules for others
and they act on his ruling,
at first he was not liable to death,
and now he is liable to death.
But when he acts on his ruling himself?
At first he was also liable to death!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first case in the ברייתא from Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that he is liable when he acts on his own ruling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Doing the sin himself already carried the death penalty before he became a זקן ממרא, so this rule seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Narrowing the question to sins with a court death penalty
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sharpens its question. For חלב and blood, which carry כרת and not court death, the ruling adds something. But for sins that carry court death, he was already liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works if he ruled about forbidden fat and blood. Before, he could not be killed by the court for those, and now he can. But if he ruled about sins that carry court death, he could already be killed before!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows exactly where its question applies. It is not a new question. The גמרא is narrowing the challenge from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some sins, like eating חלב or blood, carry כרת and not court death. For those, becoming a זקן ממרא does turn him into someone the court can kill. The question still stands for sins that already carry court death, since there the death penalty is not new.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well, this is fine (in one case)
Forbidden fat and blood (sins with כרת)
Sins that carry a death penalty from the court

phrases.english: This works where he ruled about forbidden fat and blood,
where at first he was not liable to death,
phrases.notes: Eating חלב or blood carries כרת, not a death penalty from the court.

phrases.english: and now he is liable to death.
But where he ruled
about sins that carry a court death penalty,
at first he was also liable to death!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the challenge from Step 13 to the case where it really applies.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that he is liable when he acts on his own ruling, in the case of sins that carry court death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The question does not apply to חלב and blood, where the death penalty is new. It still applies to sins that already carry court death.

steps.title: The difference is the warning
steps.stepSummary: Before he became a זקן ממרא, he could be put to death only if he was warned first. Now he can be put to death even without a warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Before, he needed a warning. Now he does not need a warning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Even for sins that carry court death, becoming a זקן ממרא changes something real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the court can put someone to death only if he was warned (התראה) right before the sin. As a זקן ממרא, he is put to death even without that warning. So the ברייתא's rule does add something.

keyTerms.meaning: A warning given before the sin, normally needed before the court can punish
Needs, requires

steps.whatToRemember: Even when the sin already carries death, a זקן ממרא who acts on his ruling is different. He can be put to death without the usual warning (התראה).
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the law of the זקן ממרא is a special, stricter rule. It is not just the normal punishment for the sin he did.

phrases.english: At first, he needs a warning;
now, he does not need a warning.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעִיקָּרָא בָּעֵי הַתְרָאָה הַשְׁתָּא לָא בָּעֵי הַתְרָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge raised in Steps 13 and 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a new legal result: the warning requirement falls away.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Becoming a זקן ממרא adds nothing for a sin that already carries court death.
steps.terutzMaskana: It does add something: he can be put to death without the warning that is normally required.

steps.title: What about a מסית, who never needed a warning?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the last answer. A מסית can be put to death without a warning even before becoming a זקן ממרא, so what does the ruling add?
steps.simpleTranslation: A מסית doesn't need a warning anyway. So what can we say about him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing back on the answer from Step 15. The 'no warning needed' answer seems not to work for a מסית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the new part of being a זקן ממרא is that he can be killed without a warning. But a מסית, someone who pushes others to serve idols, is already put to death without a warning. So if the זקן ממרא ruled that a מסית is allowed and then did it himself, his status as a זקן ממרא seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who tries to persuade another person to serve idols
A warning given before a sin. Normally it is needed before a court can punish.
'What is there to say?' The question has no easy answer yet.

phrases.english: An instigator, who does not need a warning,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 15 by finding a case where the 'no warning' difference does not exist.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a זקן ממרא's new status lets him be killed without a warning.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A מסית is killed without a warning even before, so the 'no warning' difference cannot explain why the ruling matters in his case.

steps.title: Before, his excuse was accepted; now it is not
steps.stepSummary: Before he became a זקן ממרא, a מסית who gave a reason for his actions could have it accepted. After his ruling, his reason is no longer accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Before, if he gave a reason, we accepted it from him. Now, if he gives a reason, we do not accept it from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about the מסית. Something does change after he becomes a זקן ממרא: his explanation no longer saves him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the ruling, a מסית who explained why he thought his actions were allowed could be believed and let off. Once he has openly ruled that it is allowed, against the Great בית דין, his excuse is not accepted. So being a זקן ממרא still adds something, even for a מסית.

keyTerms.meaning: At first, before he became a זקן ממרא
A reason or explanation he gives for what he did
We accept it from him
Now, after he issued his ruling

steps.whatToRemember: Becoming a זקן ממרא always changes something. Usually he no longer needs a warning. For a מסית, his excuse is no longer accepted.

phrases.english: Before, if he gave a reason,
we accept it from him.
Now, if he gives a reason,
we do not accept it from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a different change in the law that applies even to a מסית.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For a מסית, being a זקן ממרא adds nothing, because he never needed a warning.
steps.terutzMaskana: It adds something: before, his explanation could save him; now it cannot.

steps.title: משנה: The Sages' explanations are treated more strictly
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה teaches that a זקן ממרא is treated more strictly for rulings about the Sages' explanations than for clear תורה laws. Denying תפילין makes him exempt, but adding a fifth box makes him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is more strictness for the words of the Sages than for the words of the Torah. If one says 'There are no תפילין,' breaking the words of the Torah, he is exempt. If he says 'five boxes,' adding to the words of the Sages, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It tells us which kinds of rulings can make an elder a זקן ממרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who denies a clear תורה law, like the מצוה of תפילין itself, is not punished as a זקן ממרא, because everyone knows the תורה says it and no one will follow him. But if he argues about a detail that comes from the Sages' explanation, such as the number of boxes in the head-תפילין, he is liable, because people might listen to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Strictness; a more severe treatment
The words of the Sages: the explanations of the Torah passed down by the Sages
Laws written clearly in the Torah
The boxes with Torah passages worn on the head and arm
The compartments in the head-תפילין. The tradition says four.

steps.confusionAlert: It sounds backwards that denying a Torah law gets no punishment. The point is only about the זקן ממרא punishment: denying something so obvious does not make him a rebellious elder, because no one would follow him.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: There is more strictness in the words of the Sages
than in the words of the Torah.
One who says: 'There are no תפילין,'

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי לַעֲבוֹר עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: so as to break the words of the Torah, is exempt.
If he says 'five compartments,'
phrases.notes: The head-תפילין have four compartments, and he's saying there should be five.

phrases.english: adding onto the words of the Sages, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ חוֹמֶר בְּדִבְרֵי סוֹפְרִים מִבְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה after the discussion of the previous one is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A זקן ממרא is exempt for denying a clear Torah law, but liable for adding to a detail that comes from the Sages' explanation.

steps.title: רבי אושעיא: Only a מצוה like תפילין fits
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא sets out the exact kind of מצוה a זקן ממרא can be liable for. Its basis is from the תורה, its details are from the Sages, and adding to it ruins it. Only תפילין fits, following רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said in the name of רבי אושעיא: He is liable only for something whose basis is from the Torah and whose explanation is from the Sages, where it is possible to add, and if one adds, he ruins it. The only example we have is תפילין, following רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a statement that narrows the משנה. It lists the conditions a מצוה must meet before a זקן ממרא can be liable for ruling about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three conditions must all be met. The מצוה itself comes from the תורה. Its details come from the Sages. Adding to it makes it invalid. תפילין fits all three: the תורה commands them, the Sages explain the four boxes, and a fifth box ruins them. This follows רבי יהודה's opinion about which rulings count.

keyTerms.meaning: Its basis or root: the basic מצוה
Its explanation: the details of how to do it
To add on
Takes away. Here: the addition ruins the מצוה.
According to the opinion of

steps.whyThisMatters: This sharply limits when a זקן ממרא can be punished. That sets up the next question: are there other מצוות that also fit these rules?

phrases.english: GEMARA: רבי אלעזר said
that רבי אושעיא said:
He is liable only for a matter
whose basis is from the words of the Torah
and whose explanation is from the words of the Sages,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ לְהוֹסִיף, וְאִם הוֹסִיף גּוֹרֵעַ.
phrases.english: and where one can add, and if he adds, he takes away.
And we have nothing like this except תפילין,
according to רבי יהודה.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and narrows the משנה's rule about תפילין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A זקן ממרא is liable only for a מצוה that is Torah-based, explained by the Sages, and ruined by adding. Only תפילין fits, following רבי יהודה.

steps.title: Doesn't לולב fit the same conditions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אושעיא. לולב seems to meet all three conditions, so why is תפילין called the only example?
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is לולב! Its basis is from the Torah, its explanation is from the Sages, one can add to it, and if he adds, he ruins it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that תפילין is the only example. It points to לולב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה commands taking the four species on סוכות, but the Sages explain which species they are and how many. Adding a fifth species ruins the מצוה. So לולב seems to meet every condition רבי אושעיא gave, which contradicts his claim that only תפילין fits.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't there...? Used to bring a counter-example.
The palm branch, together with the other species taken on סוכות

phrases.english: But there is לולב,
phrases.notes: This means the whole מצוה of the four species taken on סוכות, not just the palm branch.

phrases.english: whose basis is from the words of the Torah
and whose explanation is from the words of the Sages,

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ לְהוֹסִיף, וְאִם הוֹסִיף – גּוֹרֵעַ?
phrases.english: and where one can add, and if he adds, he takes away?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אושעיא's claim in Step 19 that only תפילין fits.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אושעיא's statement that only תפילין meets the conditions.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Gives a counter-example, לולב, that seems to meet all three conditions.

steps.title: לולב does not truly fit the rule
steps.stepSummary: Whatever view we hold about binding the לולב, adding a species never takes a good מצוה and spoils it. Either the extra species stands apart, or the bundle was faulty from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: With לולב, what do we hold? If a לולב does not need to be tied together, then each species stands alone and the extra one stands alone, so nothing is ruined. If a לולב does need to be tied, it is ruined right from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 20 and explains why לולב is not a true example of רבי אושעיא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule needs a מצוה that is complete and valid and then becomes ruined because something was added. If no tying is needed, the extra species is simply a separate object and ruins nothing. If tying is needed, the extra species is part of the bundle from the moment it is made, so there was never a valid מצוה object that later got spoiled.

keyTerms.meaning: What do we hold? It sets up two possible views.
Binding, meaning tying the species of the לולב together
This one stands by itself, so it is a separate item
Already lacking, meaning faulty from the very start

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying that adding to a לולב is fine. It is saying that the case does not match the specific pattern of a good מצוה becoming ruined, which the rule for a זקן ממרא requires.

phrases.english: With lulav, what do we hold?

phrases.aramaic: אִי סְבִירָא לַן דְּלוּלָב אֵין צָרִיךְ אֶגֶד,
phrases.english: If we hold that a lulav does not need binding,
this stands by itself
phrases.notes: "This" means the proper species he uses for the מצוה.

phrases.english: and that stands by itself.
phrases.notes: "That" means the extra species he added.

phrases.english: And if we hold that it needs binding,
it is already ruined from the start.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the לולב challenge from step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two-sided analysis: under either view, the case fails the rule's condition that an addition ruins a valid מצוה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: לולב meets all three conditions, just like תפילין
steps.terutzMaskana: Adding to a לולב either ruins nothing or adds to something already faulty, so it is not an example of the rule

steps.title: What about ציצית?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests ציצית as another מצוה that seems to fit all of רבי אושעיא's conditions.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is ציצית. Its basis is from the Torah, its details come from the Sages, it is possible to add to it, and if one adds, he ruins it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new challenge to רבי אושעיא: ציצית also seems to meet all three conditions, so תפילין should not be the only example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה commands ציצית, but the number of strings comes from the Sages' explanation. Adding extra strings seems to spoil the מצוה, which would match the pattern of תפילין exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: Fringes worn on the corners of a garment
Its basis, the main command
Words of the Sages, here meaning the Sages' explanation of the details
Takes away, meaning he ruins the מצוה

phrases.english: But there is tzitzit,
whose basis is from the words of the Torah
and whose explanation is from the words of the Sages,
and it is possible to add to it,
and if he added, he ruins it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After לולב was rejected, the גמרא raises a second possible example
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אושעיא's claim that only תפילין fits the three conditions
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ציצית seems to match every condition, so תפילין would not be the only example

steps.title: ציצית also may not fit: the first side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a two-sided answer. If the upper knot is not required by the תורה, the extra string stands apart and ruins nothing. The second side continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: With ציצית, what do we hold? If the upper knot is not from the Torah, then the proper strings stand alone and the extra string stands alone. And if we hold... (this continues).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to show that ציצית, like לולב, does not truly fit the rule. Here it gives only the first side of the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the תורה does not require the upper knot, the strings are not joined into one unit. An extra string is then just a separate thread, and it does not spoil the proper ones. This works just like the first side of the לולב answer in step 21.

keyTerms.meaning: The upper knot, tied near the edge of the garment
Not required by Torah law

phrases.english: With tzitzit, what do we hold?

phrases.aramaic: אִי סְבִירָא לַן דְּקֶשֶׁר הָעֶלְיוֹן לָאו דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא,
phrases.english: If we hold that the upper knot is not from the Torah,
this stands by itself
phrases.notes: "This" means the proper strings, and "that" in the next line means the extra string.

phrases.english: and that stands by itself.
And if we hold...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ציצית challenge from step 22 using the same two-sided method as the לולב answer
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two-sided analysis, partly given here; the second side continues
steps.terutzMaskana: First side: if the upper knot is not from the Torah, the extra string is separate and ruins nothing
